thread.title_full: Broome Bridge Demolition Delayed a Year by Endangered Mussels - NewsBreak

author: Bob Joseph
title: Broome Bridge Demolition Delayed a Year by Endangered Mussels - NewsBreak
text:
By Bob Joseph ,
8 hours ago Photo: Bob Joseph/WNBF News A bunch of mussels are preventing Broome County from removing a rusting Susquehanna River bridge that closed 35 years ago.
The county has been working a long time to clear the way for demolition of the old Center Village Bridge in the town of Colesville.
A sign at one end of the old Center Village Bridge in the town of Colesville. (Photo: Bob Joseph/WNBF News) The structure was replaced with a modern bridge in 1990. For a time, pedestrians and bicyclists were allowed to cross the old span but that was stopped due to safety concerns.
Broome County Executive Jason Garnar had expected the closed bridge would have been removed by now. But when mussels were discovered in the river around the site, the project was halted.
A view of the old Center Village Bridge from the “new” bridge on June 22, 2023. (Photo: Bob Joseph/WNBF News) Garnar told WNBF News the state Department of Environmental Conservation required the county to develop a plan to relocate the mussels while the demolition work was underway.
The county executive said the DEC has approved the plan. That’s the good news, he said. “The bad news is that we actually can’t remove the mussels until 2026.”
A close-up view of the Center Village Bridge on June 22, 2023. (Photo: Bob Joseph/WNBF News) Garnar said there are environmental reasons why they can’t be relocated now. He said “sometime in the spring or summer” the mussels can be moved.
After that, the bridge demolition can finally get underway. That’s now scheduled between August and October of next year.
The initial cost estimate for the removal of the old structure was “a couple hundred thousand dollars.” There’s no word on how much the mussel moving job will add to the cost of the project.
WNBF NEWS VIDEO: A look back to when we first visited the “forgotten” bridge in June 2023.

Remember These? The Fisher-Price Toys That Bring Back Instant Memories Whether the farm life was your thing or you were more into castles and airports, these iconic Fisher-Price toys are guaranteed to bring back a flood of childhood memories. Gallery Credit: Stephen Lenz FISHER-PRICE The Fisher-Price Phonograph This bad boy spun real records, which meant there was no reason you couldn’t drop on your dad’s Richard Pryor comedy albums. FISHER-PRICE The Fisher-Price Record Player Not to be confused with the real phonograph, this “younger” setup only played those chunky plastic records it came with — think timeless bangers like Mary Had a Little Lamb and Twinkle, Twinkle Little Star . Let’s be honest, it was basically just a music box in disguise. FISHER-PRICE Fisher-Price Chatter Telephone Before kids had smartphones, we had a rotary phone with googly eyes. Almost every kid dragged this thing all over the house — kind of like you do with your phone now, isn’t it? Oh darn! FISHER-PRICE / SEARS Fisher Price 'Play Family School' This multi-tasking beast of a toy — chalkboard, magnetic letters, the works — actually made school fun, but only when you played it at home. That iconic bell on top? It meant class was in session, and it drove your parents absolutely nuts. FISHER-PRICE Fisher-Price Two Tune TV Kids today laugh at the idea of not having a screen in their room, but this was our only option. Two stories — London Bridge and Row, Row, Row Your Boat — “scrolled” past the screen, and it felt like we were watching Carson in our very own apartment.
Watch it in action below:
FISHER-PRICE Fisher-Price A-Frame House For kids who didn’t always get the chance to take a vacation, this iconic Fisher-Price A-Frame made it feel like you were off at a ski lodge or tucked away at a lakeside getaway. FISHER-PRICE Fisher-Price Play Family Castle This castle gave you a chance to go medieval during playtime. With a working drawbridge, a secret trap door, and a hidden dungeon with a real working door, this castle was the perfect backdrop for epic battles and daring rescues. FISHER-PRICE Fisher-Price Play Family Airport The Fisher-Price Play Family Airport brought big-world travel to kid-sized playtime. With its working baggage carousel and that unforgettable red plane, takeoffs and landings felt epic — even if the trips were only between the kitchen and the living room. FISHER-PRICE Fisher-Price Play Family Camper The Fisher-Price Play Family Camper made every kid feel like they were hitting the open road. With the genius canoe that acted as a camper roof, it turned the backyard into a family vacation, even during a gas crisis. FISHER-PRICE Fisher-Price Parking Garage With its spiral ramp ("Watch out below!"), working elevator complete with a bell, and a tiny service station, your Matchbox cars always had the perfect place to park — and race right back out again. FISHER-PRICE / SEARS Fisher-Price Farm Was there any sound more iconic from childhood than the “Moo!” when you opened the doors to this toy barn? From a silo that looked like a Thermos to a hayloft with sliding doors and all the farm animals you could want, every day was a day on the farm — without the manure. FISHER-PRICE Fisher-Price Play Family House This little starter home might be the reason you love browsing houses on Zillow today. With its ringing front doorbell, pint-sized furniture, and swing-open design, it was the coziest place on the block. FISHER-PRICE ADVENTURE PEOPLE Fisher-Price Adventure People The Fisher-Price Adventure People were action figures that celebrated everyday heroes instead of caped crusaders. FISHER-PRICE Fisher-Price Adventure People From pilots to investigative journalists to park rangers, these figures turned backyard adventures into something cooler than ever.

These Deliciously Retro Food Photos Will Make You Hungry for the '70s From perfectly chilled shrimp cocktail to fast food that felt like a night out, '70s food wasn’t just about eating, it was a full-on cultural moment. Gallery Credit: Stephen Lenz Getty Images/iStockphoto Retro Food Mom rocked a head-to-toe scotch plaid ensemble while cooking with the iconic floral cookware, because it was the '70s and as many patterns as possible in one room was a must. Getty Images Retro Food A plaid thermos and a rusted metal lunchbox (it was your dad's from the '60s) packed with a PB&J and some tepid milk. Anyone else's mom put hot water and a wiener in the thermos? Hot dog lunch! Getty Images Retro Food '70s folks and their indestructible cars fill the lot at this Eugene, Oregon, Denny's in 1977 — most likely with Grand Slams on the brain. Getty Images Retro Food The classic cash register, with all its buttons and loud sounds, was just as much a part of the '70s diner experience as the food itself. You couldn't leave the joint without everyone knowing you paid. Getty Images 2409237 Pulling off busy I-90 in Rapid City, South Dakota, never looked so good, because you knew you were about to eat some good stuff out of paper wrappers and cardboard containers, since styrofoam didn't appear until the late '70s. Getty Images/iStockphoto Retro Food Bold orange vinyl booths were the unofficial seating of '70s fast food joints, and if it was a sticky summer with no A/C, you knew your sweaty legs in short shorts were going to cause a loud ruckus when you got up to leave. Getty Images/iStockphoto Retro Food If Mom pulled out the good floral cookware, you knew the house was about to be filled with the smell of something casserolish, bubbly, and unmistakably '70s. Getty Images Retro Food This Marlo Thomas look-alike is all smiles with her Jell-O mold in hand because she knew there was no '70s party actually happening without a jiggly-wiggly showstopper of a gelatin dessert on the table. Getty Images Retro Food When beige was a flavor... This spread may look bland, but in the '70s, it meant the party was about to start, and the spray cheese was next to show up. Getty Images/iStockphoto Retro Food Lunch on the hood, anyone? It was smiles for miles because in the '70s, family road trips meant pit stops, bagged lunches, endless candy and soda, and eating wherever and whatever the heck you wanted. Getty Images Retro Food Nothing says '70s dinner party with married friends like fondue, laughter, and maybe a bowl of keys on the side because cheese wasn't the only thing heating up at this swinging shindig in the suburbs. Getty Images Retro Food Tropical vibes, '70s-style! Nothing set the food scene like bland melon piles and a halved grapefruit -- topped, of course, with the ultimate '70s garnish: a leathery maraschino cherry. Getty Images/iStockphoto Retro Food A hearty helping of meatloaf and instant mashed potatoes, but don't forget the frozen veggie medley because this is the '70s. Getty Images Retro Food The '70s were all about serving suave looks (and burgers). Getty Images/iStockphoto Retro Food A truly festive spread, egg salad with tomato wedges and a celebratory ham, a '70s staple (the pineapple rings and cherries were likely just removed). Add to the mix: gloriously '70s yellow wallpaper. Getty Images Retro Food Nautical themes were so '70s. Fruit cocktail with cherries (again!), enough whipped topping to sink a ship, this buffet is a full-on '70s sea-worthy spectacle. Getty Images Retro Food It almost looks like the people from the iconic "I'd Like to Buy the World a Coke" commercial decided to have a tropical-themed seaside clam bake, which is also very '70s. Getty Images Retro Food Nothing says "We're married!" like a wedding cake topped with Precious Moments-style figurines. Wedding food has come a long way since the '70s, but you just know these two have been sitting in a curio cabinet somewhere in the Midwest, patiently waiting to be passed down to the granddaughter. Getty Images Retro Food In the '70s, turkeys were often more lacquered wood than actual bird, and this one is a perfect specimen. All that’s missing is the hum of an electric carving knife and the smell of Grandpa’s pipe. Getty Images/iStockphoto Retro Food Back in the '70s, airplane food wasn't just edible, it was freakin' fancy. White linens, real silverware (imagine that today) and a dash of Pan Am prestige, eating while flying felt more like fine dining. Getty Images Retro Food Nothing says 'summer fun in the '70s' like a sweaty camper, a smoking hot grill (no doubt lighter fluid was involved), and a folding table topped with red gingham. You can smell the hot dogs and taste the RC Cola now. Getty Images/iStockphoto Retro Food Shrimp cocktail was the pinnacle of '70s sophistication. Chilled to perfection, served in what looked like a pudding cup filled with zesty cocktail sauce (the kind that would give you heartburn today), and served with a side of “You've come a long way, baby!” Getty Images Retro Food The faux wood rolling buffet setup meant that you were at a '70s school banquet. Your hands are already feeling sweaty. No doubt there was some Salisbury steak, buttery rolls, and watery green beans coming your way. It was all a much-needed distraction when you still couldn't work up the nerve to ask Marsha/Linda/Tammy to slow dance.
